---
title: "Capstone — your own LLM application"
subtitle: "Day 4 · pick a track, build it, and defend the evidence"
---

Murshid has been the worked example all week: every module explained a discipline
and then showed it running in one bilingual citizen-services assistant. The
capstone is where you build **your own** application with the same disciplines —
**in one Colab notebook**, the same way every lab this week ran.

You are the application engineer of record. A review board — an architect, a
security assessor and a service-delivery director — approves a pilot on evidence:
a working notebook, an evaluation report with calibrated numbers, and a cost
model that survives national-scale arithmetic.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## One notebook, zero setup — the same template the labs already used

No Docker, no CI pipeline, no local install. Your submission is **one Colab
notebook** (plus a couple of small supporting files if you want them — your own
golden-set data, your own prompt-version files) that opens with a setup cell
modeled on the one every lab this week already used: on Colab it clones your
repo, installs what it needs, and starts a backend with no API key required by
default. If a stranger opens your notebook link and hits **Runtime → Run all**,
it should reach a working conversation with nothing else installed. That *is*
your reproducibility proof — there is no separate CI pipeline to keep green.
:::

## Choose one track

Pick one. Each is a shape that genuinely needs everything the week covered — a
router, validated structure, tools of different risk classes, a bilingual guard
wall, a golden set, and a cost model. Whichever you pick, the rubric below applies
in full.

| Track | The application | What makes it need the whole week |
|---|---|---|
| **A · Citizen services** | Renewals, fees, documents, appointments for a fictional authority | The course's own reference shape: grounded FAQ, a booking that acts, an escalation path |
| **B · Campus services** | Admissions, enrolment, transcripts and advisor appointments | Facts that must be quoted exactly, a side-effecting booking, and a student-privacy problem |
| **C · Internal IT service desk** | Access requests, asset bookings, incident triage and hand-off to a human | Authorisation is the whole game: who is asking decides what may be done |
| **D · Retail order support** | Order status, returns, exchanges, store appointments | Order lookups are read-only, returns act, and the catalogue is the grounding |

::: {.callout-important}
## Murshid is the example, not the submission

You may read, borrow patterns from, and copy plumbing out of `murshid/` — that is
what a reference implementation is for. You may **not** submit Murshid with the
service directory swapped. The domain, the tools, the corpora, the golden set and
the guards must be yours, because every rubric section below is scored on evidence
you produced about **your** traffic.

If your idea does not fit any of the four tracks, propose it on Day 1. Anything
with grounded answers, at least one action that changes something, and a reason to
refuse is likely fine.
:::

The capstone is graded on **7 sections, 100 points, pass at 70, distinction at
90**. There is no per-section floor, but there is one rule that overrides
everything else — see the callout below.

This page maps each section to the module that teaches it, states what full marks
looks like, and names the mistake that most often costs the points.

::: {.callout-important}
## Read this first

Most lost marks are **not** from difficult work done badly. They are from a
requirement nobody noticed — a deliverable that was never attempted, or one that
was written about but never actually run. Go through this page before you start,
and again before you submit.

**And one rule is absolute.** A capstone whose **safety suite is red at
submission cannot pass**, whatever it scores elsewhere. The safety cases test
your guards, which are your code, run as cells in your notebook. A red safety
suite is not bad luck with a model.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Where "commonly lost on" comes from

This course has not run a cohort yet, so unlike the older programmes these are not
yet patterns observed in submissions. Each one is an anti-pattern named explicitly
by the module that teaches the section, or one of the four flags below that caps a
criterion. The first cohort will sharpen them.
:::

## The seven sections

### 1. Architecture and the model boundary — 15 pts

**Where:** [Module 1 — architecture patterns](modules/m1-architecture.qmd) ·
[Module 2 — APIs and open weights](modules/m2-apis-and-open-weights.qmd)

**Full marks:** router-first design — FAQ single-call, service workflow with tools,
escalation to a human. **Every** model call through your `LLMClient` boundary,
proven with an `assert` cell in your notebook: no provider SDK import appears
anywhere outside one clearly-marked adapter section — the same claim
`tests/test_architecture.py` makes in the course repo, run inline instead of in
CI. Two live backends, one commercial and one open-weight, **switchable by config
rather than by code**. Reliability demonstrated under a real, scripted fault — a
rate-limit and an outage, faked the way `FakeClient` does in Lab 1 — with the
transcript captured as notebook output. One ADR (a notebook section, or a
separate `DECISIONS.md` if you prefer) recording the pattern and the model
choices.

**Commonly lost on:** a provider SDK imported somewhere outside your one adapter
section "just to test." A reader going through your notebook top to bottom will
find it, and the whole course rests on the claim it protects. Second most likely:
a fallback chain that exists in config and has never once been exercised — if you
cannot show the fault transcript, it did not happen.

### 2. Structured outputs and function calling — 15 pts

**Where:** [Module 3 — structured outputs and tools](modules/m3-structured-outputs-and-tools.qmd)

**Full marks:** one validated request object for your domain — a ticket, an
enrolment, a return — extracted with the validate → retry → repair loop, and
**measured** pass rates split by language. At least three tools spanning the risk
classes: one read-only, one side-effecting behind an authorisation gate that reads
the authenticated session, one terminal. A bounded loop. Your own negative
tool-safety cases, run as `assert` cells that each print pass/fail, all green.
Every tool call logged with its risk class and loop iteration.

**Commonly lost on:** authorisation that lives in the prompt or in the tool
description rather than in `session.authorize()`. Anything inside the token stream
is something an attacker can write to, and Module 4 exists to make that concrete.
Also: relaxing the schema to `str` so a failing corpus goes green — that is the
validation wall dismantled, and it reads as a fix in the diff.

### 3. Prompt pipeline and guardrails — 15 pts

**Where:** [Module 4 — prompts and guardrails](modules/m4-prompts-and-guardrails.qmd)

**Full marks:** every prompt a versioned artefact — files in your repo, or clearly
labelled sections in your notebook — with a changelog, **zero inline prompt
text**, and the served version recorded in your logging. The five-stage pipeline
with each stage demonstrated alone in its own cell. Attack corpus (**≥ 30 cases,
bilingual**) **≥ 95% blocked with 0% false positives** on a legitimate corpus of
the same size (≥ 30 cases, with deliberate traps). Canary intact; refusals
designed, bilingual, and never echoing the payload.

**Commonly lost on:** reporting a block rate without its false-positive pair. It is
one of the four capping flags, and it is the easiest to avoid — the two numbers come
out of the same cell. Close behind: patterns matched against raw text instead of
normalised text, which quietly lets every Arabic and homoglyph payload through a
guard that looks correct.

### 4. Evaluation harness — 20 pts

**Where:** [Module 5 — evaluation](modules/m5-evaluation.qmd)

**Full marks:** a golden set of **≥ 40 cases**, stratified by intent, language,
difficulty and risk, Arabic-majority, safety oversampled, every stratum ≥ 8 cases
and every expectation owner-approved (that's you). The harness runs the **real**
pipeline — the functions your notebook actually calls, not a simplified copy.
Deterministic asserts carry every safety claim; the judge is calibrated to
**Cohen's κ ≥ 0.6** with the evidence included. Safety stratum 100%. A
regression-gate **function**, demonstrated blocking a seeded change: run it once
clean and once against a deliberately-degraded prompt, both outputs captured in
the notebook, reading slices rather than the average. An Evaluation Report (a
notebook section, or `EVALUATION_REPORT.md`) generated from real runs, including
known limitations.

**Commonly lost on:** editing golden cases so failures pass. The set should be
diffable against whatever generated it, and this is the one dishonesty this
course cares most about. Also frequent: a judge wired to a gate with no
calibration run at all — a κ = 0.3 judge blocking merges is a random-number
generator with authority.

### 5. Cost and latency engineering — 15 pts

**Where:** [Module 6 — cost, latency and caching](modules/m6-cost-latency-caching.qmd)

**Full marks:** a meter covering **100%** of model calls, guards and router
included. Prompt-cache discipline proven by `usage.cached_input_tokens` rather than
asserted, at ≥ 65% of input tokens cached. A response cache whose key carries
everything that changes an answer, with a semantic tier thresholded on measured
data and **zero wrong hits** on your own near-miss suite. A before/after cost
table (a notebook section, or `BENCHMARKS.md`) showing **≥ 60% cost reduction**
with the eval verdict recorded beside every step.

**Commonly lost on:** a saving with no eval verdict next to it — the third capping
flag, and the whole point of the module's one sentence. Also: optimising before
metering, which reliably produces a week of work on the 4% line item while the 92%
one sits unexamined.

### 6. Model comparison and recommendation — 10 pts

**Where:** [Module 2](modules/m2-apis-and-open-weights.qmd) ·
[Module 5](modules/m5-evaluation.qmd) ·
[Module 6](modules/m6-cost-latency-caching.qmd)

**Full marks:** both backends run over **your own** golden set, reported by slice
rather than as one number, with cost and latency alongside quality. A self-host
break-even computed from throughput **you measured**, and a routing recommendation
that follows from both. Recorded in your decisions section with the evidence
attached.

**Commonly lost on:** quoting a leaderboard or a vendor throughput figure instead
of measuring on your own traffic. The recommendation is only worth points because
it is re-runnable; a number you did not produce cannot be re-run.

### 7. The application, complete — 10 pts

**Where:** all six modules, integrated

**Full marks:** your notebook, opened fresh in Colab and run top to bottom
(**Runtime → Run all**), reaches a working bilingual conversation with **zero
setup** — no clone, no local install, no key required by default. A five-minute
live walkthrough of your notebook's own cells, exercising four things live — a
grounded answer, a tool-completed action, a refused attack, and a graceful
fallback — then one adversarial question from the floor, answered by re-running
the relevant cell.

**Commonly lost on:** a notebook that only runs because of local state left over
from a previous run. Restart the runtime and run it fresh, top to bottom, before
you submit — the same discipline Colab already forces on every lab this week.

## Pick one extension

| Extension | What it proves |
|---|---|
| **Conversation-summarisation memory** | the third state strategy from Module 1, with eval cases showing long conversations retain key facts |
| **A cascade on your busiest route** | cheap-first with a deterministic escalation signal, measured against your own router baseline |
| **Batch mode** | overnight re-answering of your golden set through a batch path, with the cost comparison |
| **A guard dashboard** | attack attempts, verdict layers and a false-positive review queue, rendered from your logs |
| **A second open-weight model** | a size or quantisation comparison on the self-hosted route, with throughput and quality slices |
| **Indirect-injection hardening** | a poisoned tool result caught by the outbound wall, with five corpus cases proving it |

Extensions add up to **+5** (capped at 100), and only if mandatory scope scores
≥ 80. An extension is not a way to buy back a weak section.

## Deliverables

1. **Repository URL** with full history — your build visible as commits rather
   than one bulk upload — holding your notebook and any small supporting files.
   No CI is required; the reproducibility proof is the notebook itself, restarted
   and run fresh.
2. **An Evaluation Report** (a notebook section, or `EVALUATION_REPORT.md`) —
   overall and sliced results for both backends, judge calibration evidence,
   safety suite status, and **known limitations**.
3. **A benchmarks table** (a notebook section, or `BENCHMARKS.md`) — the Module 2
   provider comparison, Module 3 pass rates, Module 4 guard rates (both numbers),
   Module 6 before/after.
4. **A decisions record** (a notebook section, or `DECISIONS.md` and ADRs) —
   pattern choice, model and routing choice with the break-even, and **one
   trade-off you reversed and why**.
5. **A five-minute live walkthrough** — the four-part demonstration above, run
   live from your notebook, then one adversarial question from the floor.

## How this is graded

**Your artefacts are read first, and the demo second.** The course's thesis is that
the notebook proves the system: its own execution history, the Evaluation Report,
meter output, corpus numbers.

**Presence is not effect.** A library imported but never called, a guard nothing
runs, a gate that cannot fail, or a golden case that asserts nothing does not
satisfy a deliverable.

A **held-out set** is run against your pipeline (the functions your notebook
defines) before the demos. A large gap between your reported numbers and that run
is the first discussion point, not an automatic penalty — hill-climbing
contamination is teachable, and the conversation is worth more than the
deduction.

**Four flags cap a criterion at 70%:**

- golden cases edited to make failures pass;
- guard numbers reported without the false-positive pair;
- cost savings with no eval verdict beside them;
- a judge gating anything without calibration evidence.

The floor question in the demo is deliberately adversarial — an injection attempt,
or an out-of-directory fee question. What is graded is **the system's behaviour and
your reading of its logs**, not whether the model happened to be graceful. Expect
also to be asked to break something live: lower the semantic threshold, unpin a
model, drop a guard layer. Show which gate catches it.

| Section | Points |
|---|---|
| 1 · Architecture and the model boundary | 15 |
| 2 · Structured outputs and function calling | 15 |
| 3 · Prompt pipeline and guardrails | 15 |
| 4 · Evaluation harness | 20 |
| 5 · Cost and latency engineering | 15 |
| 6 · Model comparison and recommendation | 10 |
| 7 · The application, complete | 10 |

## GitHub &amp; documentation requirements

These apply to **every project in every SDAIA Academy programme**, on top of the
seven sections above, and they are part of how the project is evaluated — not
paperwork. Your repository must include:

- A clear, comprehensive **project description**
- A **professional README** — the project idea, plus how to open and run the
  notebook
- Proper **technical documentation**
- Good **Git practices** — meaningful, incremental commits, a sane structure, and a
  `.gitignore` that excludes secrets and generated files
- A statement of **which training programme** the project was completed under
  (programme name + cohort dates)
- A link to **[SDAIA Academy's GitHub](https://github.com/SDAIAAcademy)** where
  relevant

Every trainee needs an active GitHub account, and projects are expected to stay
documented and updated there.

*Encouraged, not scored:* star and follow strong Saudi repositories and accounts,
contribute to open source, engage through forks, pull requests and issues, and
share standout projects with the community.

## The write-up

One short paragraph per section, saying which approach you took and why. This is
how understanding is verified, and it is worth real marks on its own.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Write it from your results, not from your plan

Graders check the write-up against the code and the captured output. Claims that
contradict your own artefacts are worse than an admitted gap — and on this course
they are unusually easy to spot, because almost every claim has a cell behind it.
A write-up saying the guard blocks 100% sits next to a guard-eval cell that says
otherwise; a claimed 60% saving sits next to a benchmarks table that does not show
it.

If something did not work, say so and describe what you inspected instead. An
honest gap costs a few points. A claim your own output contradicts costs
credibility across the whole submission — and your Evaluation Report has a **known
limitations** section precisely so that honesty has somewhere to live.
:::

## Before you submit

- [ ] **Your full name is in the README.** Submissions without names are not
      graded — this is not a formality.
- [ ] Your test cells all green, and **the safety stratum at 100%**. A red safety
      suite cannot pass.
- [ ] Re-read your own notebook: no provider SDK import outside your one adapter
      section, no unbounded `max_tokens`, no inline prompt text.
- [ ] Both backends actually run, switched by config, and you have shown it.
- [ ] The fault-drill transcript is captured as notebook output — the fallback
      really fired, not just written about.
- [ ] Guard numbers reported **in pairs**: block rate *and* false-positive rate.
- [ ] Judge calibration evidence included, with κ stated.
- [ ] The regression-gate function demonstrated blocking the seeded change, with
      the slice table.
- [ ] Every cost row in your benchmarks table carries its eval verdict.
- [ ] The break-even quotes **both** comparisons, not just the flattering one.
- [ ] Your Evaluation Report has its known-limitations section, and it is honest.
- [ ] Restarted the Colab runtime and run your notebook fresh, top to bottom, with
      no leftover local state.
- [ ] No API key in the notebook or in git history.
- [ ] No `TODO` or template placeholder text left anywhere.
- [ ] Your **track** is stated explicitly, and your chosen extension if you did one.
- [ ] **README** covers the project description and how to open and run the
      notebook, `.gitignore` excludes secrets, and the programme name and cohort
      dates are stated.
